title: You Thought Faith Would Make the Storm Stop. Jesus May Be Teaching You Who He Is While It Still Rages.
paragraphs: You Thought Faith Would Make the Storm Stop. Jesus May Be Teaching You Who He Is While It Still Rages.
Maybe the greatest miracle in your storm will not be how quickly Jesus changes what is happening around you—but how deeply you discover who He is while everything around you is still shaking.
There is a kind of disappointment Christians rarely admit out loud.
You prayed.
You believed.
You tried to obey God.

You stopped running from Him. You opened your Bible again. You started praying when nobody was watching. You surrendered things you once defended. You whispered the name of Jesus through tears because sometimes His name was the only prayer you had enough strength to pray.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps without realizing it, you began expecting the weather to change.
Surely following Jesus would make this easier.
Surely obedience would prevent this kind of pain.

Surely faith would mean the diagnosis changed, the marriage healed, the child came home, the bills were paid, the anxiety disappeared, the betrayal was repaired, the grief became manageable, the door finally opened.
Surely Jesus would stop the storm.
But the wind kept blowing.
And now you are carrying a question you may be almost ashamed to ask:
“Jesus… if You are really with me, why is this still happening?”
That question is older than your suffering.
And one night on the Sea of Galilee, terrified disciples essentially asked it too.
Mark tells us that after Jesus had been teaching, He said to His disciples:
“Let us go across to the other side.”
They took Him in the boat.
Then everything changed.
Mark 4:37 describes a “great windstorm.”
The Greek is startling:
λαῖλαψ μεγάλη ἀνέμου — lailaps megalē anemou
A great, violent windstorm.
This was not an inconvenient drizzle interrupting a pleasant evening.
The waves were crashing into the boat so aggressively that the vessel was already filling with water.
And Jesus?
He was asleep.
That detail hurts differently when you have suffered.
Because sometimes the most painful part of the storm is not the storm.
It is what feels like the silence of God inside it.
You can survive people misunderstanding you.
You can survive someone walking away.
You can survive financial uncertainty, sleepless nights, bad news, rejection, disappointment and seasons when nothing seems to make sense.
But when heaven seems silent while your boat is filling with water?
That can shake something much deeper.
The disciples woke Jesus and cried:
Διδάσκαλε, οὐ μέλει σοι ὅτι ἀπολλύμεθα;
Didaskale, ou melei soi hoti apollymetha?
“Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?”
Notice what fear did.
The storm outside them became an accusation inside them.
The question was no longer merely, “Will we survive?”
It became:
“Do You care?”
And perhaps that is where this story suddenly becomes yours.
Because suffering has a way of putting God on trial in the courtroom of our frightened hearts.
“Lord, do You care?”
“If You cared, why did You allow this?”
“If You loved me, why did You not prevent it?”
“If You heard my prayers, why has nothing changed?”
“If I really belonged to You, why am I still hurting?”
There are believers reading these words who do not need somebody to tell them to “just have more faith.”
You have faith.
You are simply tired.
There is a difference.
You still believe Jesus is Lord, but your hands are trembling.
You still know Scripture, but tonight the verses feel harder to hold.
You still worship, but sometimes your worship sounds more like weeping.
You have not abandoned Christ.
You are trying to find Him through the rain.
And Mark 4 contains something desperately important for people like you:
The presence of a storm is not proof of the absence of Christ.
Jesus was in the boat.
And the storm still came.
Do not miss that.
The disciples were not in that storm because they had disobeyed Jesus.
They were there after following His instruction.
Jesus Himself had said:
“Let us go across to the other side.”
Sometimes obedience leads you directly into circumstances you would never have chosen for yourself.
That destroys a dangerous version of Christianity which quietly teaches that enough faith should produce a sufficiently comfortable life.
Scripture never promises that.
Jesus Himself told His disciples, “In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16:33).
Paul endured beatings, imprisonment, rejection, hunger, shipwreck and suffering while faithfully serving Christ.
Peter wrote to believers experiencing fiery trials.
James told Christians not if but when they encountered various trials.
And our Savior did not walk toward earthly comfort.
He walked toward a cross.
Christian faith is not a contract promising that nothing terrible will happen to you.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ and the astonishing promise that whatever comes, you ultimately belong to Him.
That changes the meaning of the storm.
Not necessarily its immediate intensity.
But its ultimate authority.
The disciples shook Jesus awake.
Then Mark says:
“He arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still.”
The Greek preserves the force of His command:
Σιώπα, πεφίμωσο — Siōpa, pephimōso.
“Be silent. Be still.”
The One who appeared to be doing nothing was never powerless.
The One who seemed unaware was never unaware.
Jesus stood before something the disciples could not control and spoke as its Lord.
The wind ceased.
There was a great calm.
But strangely, Jesus did not immediately congratulate His disciples.
He asked them:
“Why are ye so fearful? how is it that ye have no faith?”
This does not mean mature Christians never experience fear.
Scripture repeatedly shows faithful people frightened, grieving, confused and overwhelmed.
The deeper issue is what fear convinces us to believe about God.
The disciples had interpreted Jesus’ apparent inactivity as indifference.
“Do You not care?”
But Jesus cared before He stood up.
He cared while He slept.
He cared while the waves were crashing.
He cared while the boat was filling.
His care did not begin when the circumstances changed.
And somebody desperately needs that truth today.
Jesus does not begin loving you when your storm ends.
He is not waiting for your situation to improve before becoming faithful.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that He has abandoned you.
Your tears are not evidence that Christianity failed.
Your suffering is not necessarily evidence that you somehow missed God.
Sometimes faith looks less like standing triumphantly on top of the waves and more like whispering from the bottom of the boat:
“Jesus, I am terrified… but I am still here.”
Maybe you expected faith to make you fearless.
But biblical faith is often trusting God while fear is still screaming.
Maybe you thought strong Christians never cried.
Jesus wept.
Maybe you thought faithful Christians never questioned.
The Psalms contain anguished questions addressed directly to God.
Maybe you believed following Jesus meant eventually reaching a place where life could no longer break your heart.
Then you discovered that Christians still bury people they love.
Christians still receive devastating diagnoses.
Christians still experience betrayal.
Christians still lose jobs.
Christians still experience depression, loneliness, persecution, disappointment and grief.
We are not immune to a fallen world.
We have a Savior who entered it.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not God shouting instructions toward drowning humanity from the safety of heaven.
The Gospel is God coming to us.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
Jesus experienced hunger.
Exhaustion.
Rejection.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Violence.
Grief.
And ultimately crucifixion.
The cross demolishes the accusation that God cannot understand suffering.
Jesus Christ entered suffering more deeply than we can comprehend.
At Calvary, the One who commanded the Sea of Galilee did something even more astonishing.
He did not command the nails to disappear.
He did not call angels to destroy His enemies.
He did not descend from the cross to prove His identity to the mockers.
He stayed.
Not because He lacked power.
Because He was accomplishing redemption.
The sinless Son of God bore sin, giving Himself for sinners so that everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven, reconciled to God and given eternal life.
Then came the silence of the tomb.
Imagine being one of His disciples that Saturday.
Everything would have looked finished.
The Messiah dead.
The dream buried.
Hope sealed behind stone.
If Christianity ended on Saturday, despair would have had the final word.
But Sunday came.
Jesus rose.
And resurrection forever changed what Christians mean when we say God is faithful.
It means even death does not get the last sentence.
Because Scripture is filled with situations that looked final until God revealed they were not.
Peter’s denial looked like failure.
Grace rewrote him into a restored shepherd.
Paul’s persecution of Christians looked like an unforgivable scandal.
Grace transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no lifetime of religious accomplishments, no opportunity to repair his reputation, no years remaining to prove himself.
Only a dying confession of faith.
And Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not redefining sin so repentance becomes unnecessary.
Grace tells the truth about our sin and then points us toward a Savior whose mercy is greater than our ruin.
Maybe your storm has exposed things in you that calm seasons successfully concealed.
Fear.
Control.
Anger.
Bitterness.
Secret unbelief.
Hidden sin.
The desperate need to control tomorrow.
Perhaps you thought your greatest problem was the storm.
Then the storm exposed your heart.
That happened to the disciples.
After Jesus calmed the sea, Mark gives us an extraordinary reversal.
The storm stops…
but their fear increases.
Mark says:
ἐφοβήθησαν φόβον μέγαν — ephobēthēsan phobon megan.
Literally, they “feared a great fear.”
Why?
Because suddenly the storm was no longer the most frightening reality in the boat.
Jesus was.
They looked at one another and asked:
“Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
There it is.
The question beneath the entire story.
Not:
“How can I avoid storms?”
Not:
“How can I guarantee that every prayer gets the answer I want?”
Not even primarily:
“How do I become less afraid?”
But:
Who is this?
That is what the storm uncovered.
The disciples already knew Jesus as Teacher.
The storm forced them to confront something infinitely larger.
Who speaks to creation and creation obeys?
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly portray the LORD as sovereign over the raging sea. Psalm 107 describes sailors overwhelmed by storm, crying to the LORD in distress, and God stilling the storm.
So when Jesus stands in a boat and commands the wind and sea, Mark is not merely presenting an inspirational story about staying calm under pressure.
He is revealing something about Jesus.
The storm becomes a theater for Christ’s identity.
And perhaps your storm is confronting you with the same question.
Who is Jesus when the prayer has not been answered yet?
Who is Jesus when the medical report still says what it said yesterday?
Who is Jesus when the person you love still has not returned?
Who is Jesus when your finances remain frightening?
Who is Jesus when grief wakes up beside you every morning?
Who is Jesus when you have obeyed and still cannot see the other shore?
If Jesus is only valuable when He gives you the life you wanted, eventually suffering will dismantle your faith.
But if Jesus Himself is the treasure…
the storm can take much from you without taking everything.
Paul learned something like this through his own suffering.
He pleaded with the Lord three times for his “thorn” to depart.
God did not give Paul the answer Paul initially requested.
Instead came the promise:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
That is not a verse for pretending pain does not hurt.
It is a declaration that sometimes Christ demonstrates His sufficiency not by immediately removing weakness but by sustaining His people inside it.
There are miracles of deliverance.
Praise God for them.
Pray boldly for them.
Ask God to heal.
Ask Him to restore.
Ask Him to provide.
Ask Him to open impossible doors.
The Jesus of Scripture truly heals, rescues, provides and delivers according to His sovereign will.
But never turn a miracle into something God owes us.
Because sometimes He parts the sea.
Sometimes He calms the sea.
And sometimes He gives His child enough grace to endure the sea until they reach home.
Faith trusts Christ in all three.
Perhaps that is where you are right now.
Still waiting.
Still hurting.
Still praying.
Still confused.
Then hear this carefully:
You do not have to manufacture a victorious smile to prove you trust Jesus.
Bring Him your actual heart.
The frightened one.
The disappointed one.
The exhausted one.
The heart that sometimes asks, “Do You care?”
Bring that heart to Christ.
But do not merely ask Jesus to change your circumstances.
Ask Him to reveal Himself.
“Lord, show me who You are here.”
“Teach me to trust You here.”
“Expose whatever this storm is revealing in me.”
“Forgive my unbelief.”
“Keep me near You.”
“If You remove this cup, I will praise You.”
“If You ask me to walk through it longer, hold me.”
“And whatever happens, do not let suffering steal my eyes from Christ.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years trying to become good enough for God while secretly drowning beneath guilt.
Your greatest storm may not be financial, relational or physical.
It may be the knowledge of what you have done.
The affair.
The addiction.
The abortion.
The lies.
The years wasted.
The secret nobody knows.
The faith you abandoned.
The family you wounded.
The person you became when nobody was watching.
You may think Christianity is for people whose boats are clean.
It is not.
Jesus came for sinners.
The Gospel does not say, “Repair yourself and perhaps God will accept you.”
It announces that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
You cannot rewrite your past.
But Jesus can redeem a life surrendered to Him.
Your scandal does not become righteousness merely because you regret it.
Your sin needs forgiveness.
And forgiveness is precisely why the cross matters.
Bring the truth into His light.
Repent.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Come to Him.
There is grace.
Real grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace strong enough to forgive you and holy enough to transform you.
Maybe the storm outside you will stop tomorrow.
I pray it does.
Maybe the phone will ring.
Maybe the doctor will call with unexpectedly good news.
Maybe restoration will begin.
Maybe the door will finally open.
We should never become so cynical about suffering that we stop asking God for deliverance.
But perhaps tomorrow the wind will still be blowing.
If it is, Christ will not suddenly become less Lord.
That may be the sentence you need to save and return to when another dark night comes:
The continuation of the storm does not mean the suspension of the sovereignty of Jesus.
Your circumstances can still be frightening while Christ remains faithful.
You can still have questions while Christ remains Lord.
You can still cry while Christ remains good.
You can still be waiting while Christ remains present.
And one day, whether through deliverance in this life or resurrection into the life to come, every believer in Christ will discover that no storm had authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
So if this article found you while your own boat feels like it is filling with water, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.
And if the storm has exposed sin, fear, bitterness or something you have kept hidden from God and everyone else, perhaps your response is simply:
“No more hiding.”
Not because typing words earns grace.
It does not.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending.
And look around.
Somebody you know is currently smiling on Facebook while privately trying not to drown.
You may never know what sharing this article could interrupt.
A night of despair.
A crisis of faith.
A believer quietly wondering whether God has abandoned them.
A grieving mother.
An exhausted father.
A young Christian discovering that following Jesus does not make life painless.
A prodigal wondering whether there is still a road home.
It cannot.
Not because supporting a ministry earns salvation.
It never will.
And not because Christians must pay money in order to glorify God.
The Gospel forbids us from turning grace into a transaction.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping Gospel-centered truth reach more people, supporting and sharing faithful Christian ministry can be one practical expression of stewardship.
Send it privately to someone whose storm has lasted longer than they expected.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is asking the same question those frightened disciples asked:
“Jesus… do You care?”
The cross answers.
The empty tomb answers.
And the Christ who remains Lord when the waves rise answers.
Yes.
But His love does not always reveal itself by preventing every storm.
Sometimes His love carries us through one.
Sometimes His power silences the wind.
Sometimes His grace sustains trembling disciples until morning.
And sometimes the storm you begged Jesus to remove becomes the place where you finally discover that what you needed most was not a life without waves—
but a Savior whom the waves must obey.
The storm may still be writing across the sky, but it never gets to write the final sentence of a life held by Jesus.
